scale: binary pass/fail per criterion; weighted sum normalized to [0,1]

criteria.criterion: The report presents a gross-profit bridge whose components sum to the actual-minus-budget GP variance (within $1,000), not just a list of unreconciled observations.
The report identifies Product B's price cut as the single largest driver of the total gross-profit miss, ahead of volume and the overhead effect.
The report does NOT frame unit-volume decline as the primary cause of the margin miss or spend the majority of its causal narrative on volume/mix.
The report states or clearly implies that volume is the smallest of the three dollar-value drivers of the GP variance, not merely 'a factor'.

The report explicitly identifies that the one-time warehouse consolidation cost was allocated on a different basis (100% to one product) than the standard overhead pool (pro-rata by revenue), and names this as the root issue -- not merely listing the cost as a normal overhead increase.

The report connects the allocation inconsistency to the email thread's description of the consolidation as shared/company-wide infrastructure, rather than asserting the inconsistency without evidence from the source material.
The report does NOT include dollar figures, percentages, or dates that cannot be traced to the three provided source files.

The report correctly explains that the overhead dollar effect at the company level is real (driven by the one-time cost net of lower base-pool overhead from reduced revenue), distinct from which product line absorbs it.
The report recomputes the product-level margin miss under a consistent (pro-rata) allocation of the one-time cost, rather than only reporting the as-booked split.
The report states that Product B's corrected miss is larger than Product A's corrected miss -- the reverse of the as-booked figures -- and gets this direction right.
The report does NOT recommend that Product A's operations or cost structure be investigated as the primary corrective action, after having shown the corrected numbers.
The report notes that the allocation correction nets to zero at the total-company level -- i.e. it changes attribution between product lines, not the total company miss.
The corrected allocation the report proposes uses the same pro-rata-by-revenue basis already documented for the standard overhead pool, rather than an invented or unexplained alternative methodology.
The report includes a recommendation for how Q3+ reporting or allocation policy should change, not only a restatement of this quarter's corrected numbers.
The report opens with a concise executive summary stating the headline miss, the root cause, and the recommendation -- usable as a standalone summary for a time-pressed reader.
The report does NOT simply restate the prompt's instructions back as if they were findings (e.g. 'I built a bridge that ties out' with no supporting figures).
The report presents the budget / as-booked / corrected comparison for both product lines in a clearly labeled table or equivalent structured format, not only prose.
answer.json includes all eleven required keys with values of the correct type (float or string enum as specified in the prompt).
The report states any assumption made where the source material was ambiguous (e.g. choice of reallocation basis), rather than presenting an assumption as an established fact.

The report does NOT cast doubt on the standard overhead pool's allocation (which is consistent with stated policy and not part of the anomaly) or treat the entire $233,200 overhead figure as unreliable.
